1 · What happened
On 28 January 2026 Goldman Sachs Alternatives agreed to take a minority stake in The Private Office, a UK financial planning firm with over £3bn of client funds, subject to FCA approval. It is one public example of institutional capital buying into UK advice firms.
2 · How it affects the client
As advice firms merge or take private-equity backing they tend to centralise investment propositions and reduce the number of funds and managers used.
3 · What decision changes
Fund selection moves to a central investment committee; acquired firms' legacy fund holdings are reviewed.
4 · Implications for existing investments
A fund held by an acquired firm can be removed when its clients are moved to the acquirer's central proposition.
5 · Possible GSAM response (interpretation, not a GS statement)
Layer B: build relationships with consolidators' central investment teams early and offer scale pricing.
6 · Sales responsibility
Map who decides after each deal; the adviser relationship that won the business may no longer control it.
7 · Relationship-management responsibility
Watch for ownership changes at existing clients and re-earn the position with the new decision-makers.
8 · Risks and counterarguments
The TPO deal is an investment by the Alternatives business and the release does not link it to fund distribution; wider consolidation data was not sourced in this session; a manager owning a stake in an adviser raises conflict-of-interest questions.
A question to ask a client
After your recent acquisitions, how are you bringing investment propositions together, and who now owns fund selection?
Indicators to watch
Deal announcements; FCA commentary on consolidators; number of funds on consolidators' central lists.

Dutch pension funds move from defined benefit to the new contribution-based system (Wtp)

1 January 2026 (largest wave so far); deadline 1 January 2028 ✔ Verified D-R5-01

Event date
1 January 2026 (largest wave so far); deadline 1 January 2028
Publication date
2026-04-28
1 · What happened
Thirty Dutch pension funds, holding about EUR 542bn, had converted to the new system by 31 March 2026; 24 of them moved on 1 January 2026. Remaining funds must transfer accrued entitlements by 1 January 2028.
2 · How it affects the client
A fund that used to promise a fixed pension now manages personal pots by age group. Younger members can take more risk and need less interest-rate protection; older members still need stable income. The fund's hedging and return portfolios have to be redesigned around age cohorts and a solidarity reserve.
3 · What decision changes
How much interest-rate hedging to keep and for which cohorts; what goes into the return portfolio (more equities, credit, private assets); how the reserve is invested; whether the fiduciary manager and mandate structure still fit.
4 · Implications for existing investments
Long-dated swap and bond hedges can shrink for younger cohorts; existing matching mandates may be resized or re-benchmarked; reporting moves to cohort level and becomes more frequent.
5 · Possible GSAM response (interpretation, not a GS statement)
(Layer B, not a GS statement) Offer cohort-aware fixed income and return-seeking building blocks, and analysis specific to each fund's lifecycle design, rather than a generic LDI pitch. GSAM's Dutch presence since the 2022 NN IP acquisition is relevant capacity, but no public source ties a specific Wtp mandate to GSAM.
6 · Sales responsibility
For funds still to convert (2027 and 2028 waves), the opening is the portfolio redesign: asking what the new return portfolio needs that the old one lacked.
7 · Relationship-management responsibility
For existing mandates, the job is to keep the mandate fit for purpose through conversion: revised guidelines, benchmarks and reporting, and honesty if a matching mandate should shrink.
8 · Risks and counterarguments
The January 2026 wave passed calmly, so the 'forced selling' story may be overdone; estimates of future hedge reduction come from interested parties and carry wide uncertainty. Some funds keep higher hedging than the market expected. Many Dutch funds delegate to fiduciary managers, so the real buyer may be the fiduciary, not the fund.
A question to ask a client
Which of your age cohorts will hold less interest-rate hedging after conversion, and what will replace it in their return portfolio?
Indicators to watch
DNB quarterly counts of converted funds and assets; conversion dates of the largest remaining funds; long-end euro swap spreads around 1 January 2027 and 2028; insurer demand for long duration ahead of January 2027 Solvency II changes.
Sources
R5-S35 R5-S36 R5-S37

UK and EU money market fund rules: higher expected liquidity, no forced fees or gates

8 June 2026 (FCA update); UK regime targeted end-2026 ✔ Verified D-R5-02

Event date
8 June 2026 (FCA update); UK regime targeted end-2026
Publication date
2026-06-08
1 · What happened
The FCA said the Government expects to repeal the UK Money Market Funds Regulation by end-2026, with new FCA rules. Guidance will expect stable-NAV funds to hold 40% weekly liquid assets (20% for variable-NAV) and the link between liquidity thresholds and fees or gates will be removed. A European Commission report in 2026 pointed to the same 40%/20% levels as supervisory benchmarks without rewriting the EU regulation. EU-domiciled funds, about 90% of sterling MMF assets, stay on sale in the UK under an extended temporary regime pending an equivalence decision.
2 · How it affects the client
A treasurer using a stable-value fund gets a fund that holds more cash-like assets and is less likely to gate in a stress, at the cost of slightly lower yield. Continued UK access to EU funds is expected but not yet permanent.
3 · What decision changes
Whether to keep operating cash in LVNAV funds, move part to government-only (Public Debt CNAV) funds, or segment cash into operating, reserve and strategic buckets with short-duration strategies for the last.
4 · Implications for existing investments
Existing MMF holdings are unaffected day to day; yield may drift a little lower as funds hold more weekly liquidity; investment policies that reference old thresholds or 'fees and gates' triggers need updating.
5 · Possible GSAM response (interpretation, not a GS statement)
(Layer B, not a GS statement) Explain how each GS liquidity fund already sits against the new expectations, and offer cash segmentation: money market funds for daily cash, short-duration accounts for cash not needed for months.
6 · Sales responsibility
Lead with resilience and reporting (for example through the Mosaic portal) rather than yield alone; most treasurers already hold several providers, so the realistic aim is a larger share of balances.
7 · Relationship-management responsibility
Review each client's investment policy against the new rules before the client asks, and flag any share class or domicile changes early.
8 · Risks and counterarguments
Final FCA rules were not published at the cutoff, and the equivalence decision could attach conditions. Balances are driven far more by interest rates and bank deposit pricing than by regulation. Fees are thin, so a small yield difference moves large balances quickly in either direction.
A question to ask a client
Does your treasury policy still refer to liquidity fees and redemption gates as triggers, and how would you want your cash split if stable-value funds yield a little less?
Indicators to watch
FCA policy statement and interim guidance on weekly liquid assets; HM Treasury legislation; equivalence decision for EU MMFs (indicated for 2027); central bank rate path; industry sterling MMF assets.
Sources

1 · What happened
BNY and Goldman Sachs launched a solution that records 'mirror' tokens of money market fund shares on Goldman's GS DAP ledger, with subscriptions and redemptions through BNY's LiquidityDirect and BNY remaining the official record. GSAM was among the first fund managers.
2 · How it affects the client
In principle an institution could post fund shares as collateral directly instead of redeeming to cash first, keeping yield and avoiding a forced sale in stress.
3 · What decision changes
For now, little: it is an operational option for institutions that post margin, not a different fund.
4 · Implications for existing investments
No change to existing fund holdings.
5 · Possible GSAM response (interpretation, not a GS statement)
(Layer B, not a GS statement) Be able to explain plainly what tokenisation changes (transfer and collateral use) and what it does not (the fund's assets, risk and regulation).
6 · Sales responsibility
A conversation opener with derivatives users and hedge funds that post margin daily; not a reason by itself to switch provider.
7 · Relationship-management responsibility
Keep clients informed without overselling; note any availability limits by fund domicile.
8 · Risks and counterarguments
Launch coverage was US-focused; no public evidence was found on volumes or on availability for European funds or EMEA clients. Regulators in Europe have not broadly accepted tokenised fund shares as margin.
A question to ask a client
How much cash do you redeem from money market funds each month just to meet margin calls?
Indicators to watch
Regulatory acceptance of tokenised MMF shares as collateral in the UK and EU; extension to European-domiciled funds; adoption figures.

Insurance capital rules change in 2027 (EU) and the UK loosens matching-adjustment investing

EU: 30 January 2027; UK consultation 8 April 2025 ≈ Supported inference D-R5-04

Event date
EU: 30 January 2027; UK consultation 8 April 2025
Publication date
2025-04-08
1 · What happened
Amended EU Solvency II rules (Directive (EU) 2025/2) take effect on 30 January 2027. In the UK, the PRA consulted in April 2025 on a Matching Adjustment Investment Accelerator that lets insurers add self-assessed eligible assets to matching-adjustment portfolios before formal approval, within the lower of 5% of liabilities or GBP 2bn and a 24-month regularisation window.
2 · How it affects the client
An insurer chooses assets by yield after capital charge, not by yield alone. Rule changes alter which assets are 'capital-efficient' and how quickly an annuity writer can invest in new private asset types.
3 · What decision changes
Allocation to long-dated and private credit assets; how much to outsource; which managers can structure assets to be matching-adjustment eligible.
4 · Implications for existing investments
Existing portfolios are re-tested against new capital charges; some long-duration and equity positions become cheaper or dearer to hold.
5 · Possible GSAM response (interpretation, not a GS statement)
(Layer B, not a GS statement) Show the capital-adjusted return of proposed assets under the client's own regulatory basis; GSAM describes 'capital-efficient investment strategies' and asset-liability advice as part of its insurance offer.
6 · Sales responsibility
Sales must speak the insurer's language (capital charge, book yield, liability matching) before talking about products.
7 · Relationship-management responsibility
Relationship managers coordinate regulatory reporting data and help the client evidence eligibility of assets already held.
8 · Risks and counterarguments
The final UK policy statement and the detailed EU changes were not read in this research, so details must be checked before quoting. Regulators are also wary of private-asset concentration at annuity writers. Survey intentions to raise private assets may not turn into allocations.
A question to ask a client
Which assets in your portfolio become more or less capital-efficient under the January 2027 rules?
Indicators to watch
PRA policy statement on the accelerator; EIOPA and Commission delegated acts before January 2027; insurers' reported private-asset allocations.

Insurers are looking for extra yield from illiquid, often investment-grade, private credit while worrying about the cycle and valuations.

The survey is itself a sales and credibility tool: it gives a reason to open a conversation with a CIO using peer data.

Use the peer data in portfolio reviews to test, not to push, the client's current allocation.

It is a survey run by a manager that sells these assets, and it measures intentions. No EMEA breakdown was found on the pages read. Rising recession expectations cut against adding illiquid credit.

2026-11-05

2026-11-05
1 · What happened
The Bank of England raised Bank Rate by 0.25pp to 4% (8-1; one member wanted 4.25%), its first increase since 2023, with CPI at 3.5% and projected near 5% by mid-2027. The Fed held at 3.75-4.00% on 28 Oct with two dissents for a hike; the ECB held its deposit rate at 2.50% after a September increase.
2 · How it affects the client
Higher yields lower the present value of DB liabilities and of existing bonds; cash and money market yields rise; leveraged borrowers and floating-rate private credit face higher servicing costs; inflation-linked liabilities grow.

DB trustees: hedge ratios, collateral buffers, timing of buyout. Treasurers: how much to hold in MMFs versus term. Insurers: reinvestment yields versus credit risk. Wealth selectors: duration and cash allocations.
4 · Implications for existing investments
Mark-to-market losses on long-dated bonds; collateral calls on leveraged LDI (buffers are larger than in 2022); liquidity balances may grow.
5 · Possible GSAM response (interpretation, not a GS statement)
(Layer B, not a GS statement) Explain funding-level and collateral effects scheme by scheme; show liquidity and short-duration options; avoid presenting a rate view as certainty.
6 · Sales responsibility
A reason to open a conversation about liquidity, inflation protection or collateral resilience, not proof that a product should be bought.
7 · Relationship-management responsibility
Proactive calls to existing clients on what the move did to their portfolio and hedges, before they ask.
8 · Risks and counterarguments
The inflation projection may prove wrong and policy could reverse; schemes that are well hedged may need to do nothing; higher cash yields compete with every fee-bearing product.
A question to ask a client
How did your funding level and collateral headroom move this month, and has that changed your timetable or your liquidity needs?
Indicators to watch
17 December 2026 MPC; gilt yields and index-linked breakevens; CPI prints; any LDI collateral stress reports.

Mercer: 73% of managers use AI for operational efficiency; only 5% let it act autonomously. Isio: 85% of UK fiduciary managers use AI, mainly to draft reports and emails.
2 · How it affects the client
Clients may receive faster, more consistent responses; they also ask how AI is governed and whether outputs are checked.
3 · What decision changes
Due-diligence questionnaires now include AI governance; clients may shorten response deadlines.
4 · Implications for existing investments
No direct portfolio effect.
5 · Possible GSAM response (interpretation, not a GS statement)
(Layer B, not a GS statement) Use the time saved for accuracy checks and client-specific analysis; be able to explain controls.
6 · Sales responsibility
Faster proposal turnaround is now expected, so it no longer differentiates on its own.
7 · Relationship-management responsibility
Automated reporting raises the bar for the human explanation that accompanies it.
8 · Risks and counterarguments
Survey figures are self-reported and partly vendor-sponsored; errors in AI-drafted answers create liability; no evidence yet on junior hiring effects; BCG's 25-35% cost-saving figure is an estimate.
A question to ask a client
What do you want to know about how we use AI in the material we send you, and where would you want a named person accountable?
Indicators to watch
Regulatory guidance on AI in client communications; Cerulli/Mercer follow-up surveys; reported headcount changes in distribution.
Sources
R8-S41 R8-S42 R8-S10 R8-S38 R8-S43

Private credit under strain: elevated redemptions in retail semi-liquid funds

2026-07 ✔ Verified D-R8-06

Event date
2026-07
Publication date
2026-07
1 · What happened
The Bank of England's July 2026 Financial Stability Report said risky credit markets including private credit remain vulnerable to tighter financing conditions and that redemption requests have been elevated in several retail funds, with some limiting redemptions. Blackstone reported BCRED redemption requests stayed elevated in Q3 2026 even as private-wealth AUM reached $330bn.
2 · How it affects the client
Wealth clients in semi-liquid funds may be unable to redeem on demand; insurers and pension funds reassess valuation and liquidity assumptions; rising rates add pressure on borrowers.
3 · What decision changes
Fund selectors tighten due diligence on liquidity terms, valuation policy and leverage; some pause new allocations; insurers review capital treatment.
4 · Implications for existing investments
Holders of evergreen private credit funds face queues or gates; marks may lag.
5 · Possible GSAM response (interpretation, not a GS statement)
(Layer B, not a GS statement) Lead with liquidity terms and downside cases; do not sell semi-liquid as liquid; be explicit about who the product does not suit.
6 · Sales responsibility
Selling private markets to wealth now requires proving the client understands redemption limits.
7 · Relationship-management responsibility
Tell holders early how redemption queues work and what the fund has done; this is where trust is tested.
8 · Risks and counterarguments
Stress is concentrated in particular funds and borrowers; private wealth inflows continue (Blackstone BXPE record quarter); the BoE judges households and corporates resilient in aggregate.
A question to ask a client
If you could not redeem for four quarters, would this allocation still be the right size for your clients?
Indicators to watch
BoE December 2026 FSR; redemption data from large evergreen funds; default rates; FCA/ESMA action on semi-liquid funds.
Sources
R8-S52 R8-S34 R8-S53

UK fiduciary management: fewer mandates, larger ones, falling fees at the top

2026-04 ✔ Verified D-R8-07

Event date
2026-04
Publication date
2026-04
1 · What happened
UK fiduciary assets are above £250bn (+58% in three years) but the number of mandates fell 4% in the year to June 2025, the first fall since 2008, as schemes buy out. OCIO-style mandates are 6% by number and 53% of DB fiduciary AUM. Fees above £500m are falling; below £50m they rose. Providers are consolidating (Mercer-Cardano, Nuveen-Schroders) and Columbia Threadneedle exited.
2 · How it affects the client
Large schemes have many bidders and pricing power; small schemes have fewer bidders. About 26% of fully delegated schemes expect buyout within three years, which ends the mandate.
3 · What decision changes
Whether to delegate fully, partially or not at all; whether to run on or buy out; whether to pay for independent oversight (only one in three do).
4 · Implications for existing investments
Existing fiduciary mandates shrink or terminate at buyout: a good client outcome that removes fee revenue.
5 · Possible GSAM response (interpretation, not a GS statement)
(Layer B, not a GS statement) Compete where bespoke capability matters (£1bn+); be clear about the endgame path and what happens to fees when the scheme buys out.
6 · Sales responsibility
Few, very large, slow competitive tenders run by third-party evaluators; losing after months of work is normal.
7 · Relationship-management responsibility
Help the scheme reach its endgame even though success ends the relationship; propose oversight rather than resist it.
8 · Risks and counterarguments
Goldman's UK share is not public; consultant-heritage providers hold about half of mandates by number; run-on with surplus release could slow buyouts (scenario).
A question to ask a client
Is your endgame buyout or run-on, and how should your fiduciary manager be paid in a way that does not reward delaying it?
Indicators to watch
Isio, IC Select, XPS and Quantum annual surveys; large mandate announcements; Pension Schemes Act surplus rules (see R3).
Sources
R8-S10 R8-S09 R8-S11 R8-S26

Public-private alliances and active ETFs reshape products for wealth intermediaries

2026-07-22 ≈ Supported inference D-R8-08

Event date
2026-07-22
Publication date
2026-07-22
1 · What happened
Wellington, Vanguard and Blackstone launched two public-private funds (US, July 2026); Capital Group and KKR took a public-private credit fund to Europe and Asia-Pacific via HSBC Private Bank (May 2026); Goldman agreed a T. Rowe Price partnership (Sept 2025). European active ETF assets reached about EUR 117bn at end Q3 2026, with J.P. Morgan holding about 41%; passive ETFs took about 57% of Q3 2026 European fund flows.
2 · How it affects the client
Fund selectors face more wrappers for similar exposures and must judge liquidity and layered fees; shelf space goes to firms with distribution access.
3 · What decision changes
Which vehicle (mutual fund, active ETF, evergreen fund, model portfolio) goes on the approved list; how many private-market providers to carry.
4 · Implications for existing investments
Mutual fund holdings may be switched to cheaper ETF share classes or models.
5 · Possible GSAM response (interpretation, not a GS statement)
(Layer B, not a GS statement) Offer the client's preferred wrapper where it exists; be honest where a competitor leads (for example active ETFs).
6 · Sales responsibility
Approved-list placement is the start: funded assets depend on adviser adoption afterwards.
7 · Relationship-management responsibility
Support advisers with training and reporting so listed funds are actually used and held appropriately.
8 · Risks and counterarguments
Active ETFs are still about 3.4% of European ETF assets; alliance funds are small at launch; fee levels are lower than the vehicles they replace (BCG).
A question to ask a client
Which wrapper do your advisers actually use for new money now, and what would make a fund you already list easier to hold?
Indicators to watch
Morningstar active ETF data; European launches by the alliances; platform shelf changes.
Sources
R8-S14 R8-S16 R8-S24 R8-S40 R8-S39 R8-S38

Global managers build presence around Gulf sovereign investors

2026-10-19 ✔ Verified D-R8-09

Event date
2026-10-19
Publication date
2026-10-19
1 · What happened
Fourteen firms announced plans for an Abu Dhabi Global Market presence in October 2026; managers there oversee more than $2.1tn globally; Capital Group obtained an ADGM licence. BlackRock is reported to plan up to $100bn of deployment via the region; Mubadala and ADIA are reported to partner with Apollo, Blue Owl and KKR in private credit; PIF anchors new vehicles for managers that open in Riyadh.
2 · How it affects the client
Sovereign investors can ask for local presence, co-investment, knowledge transfer and anchor terms; they are partners and competitors for deals as well as clients.
3 · What decision changes
Which managers receive mandates or anchor commitments, and on what conditions (local office, joint ventures).
4 · Implications for existing investments
Existing mandates may be consolidated into strategic partnerships.
5 · Possible GSAM response (interpretation, not a GS statement)
(Layer B, not a GS statement) Coverage needs partnership structures and senior access, not product pushing; local regulation and presence matter.
6 · Sales responsibility
Long, relationship-led cycles with bespoke terms; origination credit is shared across the firm.
7 · Relationship-management responsibility
Servicing includes training, secondments and co-investment flow, beyond reporting.
8 · Risks and counterarguments
Regional conflict in 2026 has affected sentiment (BoE refers to the Middle East conflict); headline commitment figures are not funded assets; Goldman-specific Gulf evidence is outside this stream (see R5).
A question to ask a client
Beyond returns, what do you want a manager to build with you locally?
Indicators to watch
ADGM/DIFC/Riyadh licence announcements; sovereign fund annual reports; anchor mandates.
Sources
R8-S57 R8-S58 R8-S52

Tokenised money market fund shares as collateral

2025-07-23 ✔ Verified D-R8-10

Event date
2025-07-23
Publication date
2026-07-13
1 · What happened
BNY and Goldman Sachs launched 'mirror' tokens of MMF shares on Goldman's digital asset platform in July 2025, with funds from BlackRock, Fidelity, Federated Hermes, BNY Dreyfus and GSAM. In July 2026 an industry group (GDF with ISDA) published sandbox work on using tokenised MMFs as collateral.
2 · How it affects the client
Treasurers and pension funds could post MMF shares as margin instead of redeeming to cash, reducing forced selling in stress.
3 · What decision changes
Whether to hold liquidity in vehicles that can be mobilised as collateral; operational readiness and legal certainty.
4 · Implications for existing investments
No change yet for most holders; adoption volumes not established.
5 · Possible GSAM response (interpretation, not a GS statement)
(Layer B, not a GS statement) Explain what is live versus pilot; keep the focus on the client's liquidity and collateral problem.
6 · Sales responsibility
A talking point with sophisticated treasury and LDI clients, not yet a mainstream product decision.
7 · Relationship-management responsibility
Help operations teams understand eligibility and custody implications.
8 · Risks and counterarguments
Legal and regulatory acceptance of tokenised collateral is incomplete; competitors participate in the same programme, so it is not exclusive; volumes may stay small.
A question to ask a client
In a margin call, how quickly can you turn your liquidity holdings into eligible collateral today?
Indicators to watch
Regulatory statements on tokenised collateral eligibility; reported volumes; UK and EU MMF reform implementation.
Sources

(Layer B) Brand, track record and distribution reach in semi-liquid private funds.

(Layer B) Ability to pair private funds with public-market, liquidity and advisory capabilities for the same intermediary.

Appendix F · Client lifecycle, stage by stage

In the application you step through these one at a time. Here they are printed in order.

Institutional mandate

Research and targeting

LC-01

In plain English
Working out which organisations might have a need the firm can genuinely meet, before anyone picks up the phone.
What happens
The team maps a market: who the asset owners are, how large they are, who advises them, which managers they use, when contracts or strategy reviews fall due, and which searches are open. Public documents do most of the work: annual reports, statements of investment principles, committee papers, consultant search notices and trade press. Prospects are ranked by fit and timing, and some are deliberately set aside.
Who leads
Sales, with consultant relations where a consultant controls access.
Who supports
Analysts, marketing and data teams; relationship managers who know related organisations.
What the junior person produces
  • One-page prospect briefing with sources and a list of what is not known
  • Tracker of contract end dates, strategy reviews and open searches
  • Map of who advises whom (consultant, independent trustee, actuary)
  • CRM clean-up: correct contacts, roles and meeting history
On the client side
Nobody yet. The prospect does not know it is being researched and owes the firm nothing.
What good execution changes for the client
The client's first conversation is with someone who already understands its structure and constraints and does not waste its time on products that cannot fit.
Failure points
  • Targeting by size alone and ignoring fit
  • Out-of-date information presented as current
  • Pursuing a search where the firm's strategy is not rated by the client's consultant
  • Treating a public document as telling the whole story
Sales versus relationship management (illustrative; varies)
Almost entirely an origination activity. Relationship managers contribute intelligence about clients that share a consultant, sponsor or trustee.
Timing
Continuous background work; intensity rises when a search is announced.

First contact and discovery

LC-02

In plain English
The first conversations, where the aim is to understand the client's problem, not to present a product.
What happens
An introduction is made directly, through a consultant or at an industry event. Early meetings are mostly questions: what the organisation is trying to achieve, what constrains it (liabilities, liquidity needs, governance time, regulation, beliefs), how decisions are made and by whom, and what has disappointed it before. The firm also decides whether it should compete at all.
Who leads
Sales.
Who supports
A product or investment specialist if the conversation turns technical; senior sponsor for very large prospects.
What the junior person produces
  • Question list tailored to the prospect
  • Meeting notes written up the same day, separating what was said from what was inferred
  • Contact map: who decides, who advises, who influences, who operates
  • Follow-up email draft with the material promised
On the client side
Usually an investment officer, pensions manager or chief investment officer; sometimes the consultant alone. They need to know quickly whether this manager is worth further time.
What good execution changes for the client
The client is asked questions that sharpen its own understanding of the problem, and is told honestly if the firm is not a good fit.
Failure points
  • Presenting before listening
  • Speaking only to one contact and mistaking their view for the organisation's
  • Promising follow-up that does not arrive
  • Failing to qualify out: continuing because a meeting was friendly
Sales versus relationship management (illustrative; varies)
Origination. Where the organisation is already a client for another mandate, the relationship manager normally makes the introduction and may lead.
Timing
From a single meeting to many months of intermittent contact.

Solution design and proposal

LC-03

In plain English
Turning what was learned into a specific proposal: which strategy, in what form, on what terms.
What happens
Sales works with portfolio managers, product specialists and sometimes a solutions team to shape a proposal: the strategy or combination of strategies, the vehicle (pooled fund or segregated mandate), benchmark and guidelines, reporting, indicative fees. Pricing outside the standard schedule needs internal approval. The proposal should state what the approach will not do as clearly as what it will.
Who leads
Sales, with the investment or solutions team owning the investment content.
Who supports
Product specialists, pricing or business management, legal for unusual terms, compliance for review.
What the junior person produces
  • First draft of proposal slides from approved content
  • Data tables: performance, risk and peer comparisons reconciled to official records
  • Fee illustration on stated assumptions
  • Version control and compliance-review log
On the client side
Investment staff and consultant. They need a proposal that addresses their stated problem and can be compared fairly with others.
What good execution changes for the client
The client receives a proposal built around its objective and constraints, with trade-offs visible, so it can make an informed comparison.
Failure points
  • A generic pitch with the client's name on the cover
  • Fees or terms quoted without approval
  • Performance shown selectively or for a different vehicle than the one proposed
  • Over-engineering: a complex solution to a simple need
Sales versus relationship management (illustrative; varies)
Origination. For an expansion of an existing mandate the relationship manager often leads because they know the guidelines and history.
Timing
Days for a standard product; months for a bespoke or multi-asset solution.

RFP and due diligence

LC-04

In plain English
The formal written stage: answering the client's questionnaire and proving that what was said is true.
What happens
The client or its consultant issues a request for proposal (RFP) and a due-diligence questionnaire (DDQ) covering organisation, team, process, performance, risk, operations, compliance, responsible investment and fees. Responses are scored. Operational due diligence may include site visits and interviews with risk, compliance and operations staff. For UK occupational schemes appointing a fiduciary manager above the regulatory threshold, a qualifying competitive tender with at least three unconnected providers is required.
Who leads
Sales owns the submission; the RFP team runs the process.
Who supports
Content owners across the firm (portfolio managers, risk, compliance, operations, legal, human resources), each approving the facts in their area.
What the junior person produces
  • Question-by-question tracker with owner, status and deadline
  • First-draft answers from the approved library, updated for the latest quarter
  • Evidence folder: policies, organisation charts, sample reports
  • Consistency check between the RFP, the presentation and the factsheet
On the client side
Consultant's research and operational due-diligence teams, the client's investment staff, sometimes procurement. They need complete, accurate and comparable answers by the deadline.
What good execution changes for the client
The client can rely on the answers when it justifies its decision, and discovers no surprises after appointment.
Failure points
  • Missed deadline or ignored format rules, which can disqualify
  • Stale library answers (old team names, old assets figures)
  • Inconsistency between documents
  • Answering a different question from the one asked
Sales versus relationship management (illustrative; varies)
Origination. In a re-tender the relationship manager is deeply involved because the incumbent's record is part of the evidence.
Timing
Typically weeks, set by the client's timetable.

Final presentation and appointment

LC-05

In plain English
The shortlist meeting, often called a beauty parade, after which the decision-makers choose.
What happens
A small number of shortlisted managers present to the decision-making body, such as a trustee board or investment committee, usually for a fixed time with questions. The consultant normally attends and may score. The team presenting is typically the senior salesperson, the portfolio manager and the person who would manage the relationship. The client then decides, sometimes on the day, and informs managers of the outcome.
Who leads
Senior sales with the portfolio manager.
Who supports
The proposed relationship manager, product specialist, team head for large mandates.
What the junior person produces
  • Rehearsal pack and timed running order
  • Bank of likely questions with agreed answers and who takes each
  • Biographies and leave-behind document
  • Post-pitch record of every question asked and the outcome, including feedback if lost
On the client side
Trustees or committee members, who may be non-specialists with limited time, plus their consultant. They need to understand the proposal, test the people and feel able to defend the choice.
What good execution changes for the client
The decision-makers understand what they are buying and what could go wrong, and meet the people they will actually deal with.
Failure points
  • Talking over the audience's level or under it
  • A portfolio manager who cannot explain simply
  • Presenting a team the client will never see again
  • Not asking for feedback after a loss
Sales versus relationship management (illustrative; varies)
Origination, but this is where the relationship manager should first appear so the handover is not a surprise.
Timing
A single meeting; the decision may follow within days or after the next governance meeting.

Legal negotiation and onboarding

LC-06

In plain English
Agreeing the contract and opening the accounts so the mandate can legally and operationally begin.
What happens
For a segregated mandate an investment management agreement (IMA) is negotiated: guidelines, benchmark, fees, reporting, liability, termination. For a pooled fund the client completes subscription documents. Client due diligence (know-your-customer and anti-money-laundering checks) is completed. Custody links, trading accounts and reporting are set up and tested.
Who leads
Onboarding or client implementation team with legal; the relationship manager coordinates the client side.
Who supports
Sales (to honour what was promised), portfolio manager (to confirm guidelines are workable), operations, compliance, tax.
What the junior person produces
  • Document checklist and status tracker
  • Chasing list for outstanding client and custodian items
  • Comparison of contract terms against the proposal, flagging differences
  • Reporting set-up specification
On the client side
Legal advisers, operations staff, custodian, sometimes the sponsor's treasury. They need a clear list of what is required and prompt answers.
What good execution changes for the client
The mandate starts on the agreed date with guidelines that say what the client intended.
Failure points
  • Promises made in the pitch that the contract does not reflect
  • Guidelines that are ambiguous or cannot be monitored
  • Slow due-diligence document collection delaying funding
  • No single owner between sales and relationship management
Sales versus relationship management (illustrative; varies)
The seam. In a handover model responsibility passes here; in a paired or single-owner model the same people continue.
Timing
Weeks to several months, driven by legal negotiation and document collection.

Funding and transition

LC-07

In plain English
The money or assets actually arrive and the portfolio is built.
What happens
The client transfers cash or existing securities. If assets come from a previous manager, a transition plan sets out how the old portfolio becomes the new one while controlling cost and market exposure; a specialist transition manager may be used. The portfolio manager invests to the target. Fee accrual starts on funded assets. The first report is produced and checked with unusual care.
Who leads
Operations and the portfolio manager, with the relationship manager as the client's single point of contact.
Who supports
Transition specialists, trading, performance and reporting teams.
What the junior person produces
  • Funding timeline with dates and responsible parties
  • Day-one confirmation to the client of what has been received
  • Check of the first report against the contract: benchmark, fee basis, guideline tests
  • Welcome pack: contacts, reporting calendar, escalation route
On the client side
Operations and finance staff, custodian, outgoing manager. They need certainty about dates, amounts and who to call.
What good execution changes for the client
The client's assets are invested as agreed without avoidable cost, and the first report is right.
Failure points
  • Funding later or smaller than announced
  • An error in the first report, which sets the tone
  • Transition costs not explained in advance
  • Performance inception date disputed
Sales versus relationship management (illustrative; varies)
Stewardship begins. An announced mandate is not fee-paying until funded, so sales often stays involved until money arrives.
Timing
Days for cash into a pooled fund; weeks or longer for a complex transition or phased funding.

Ongoing reviews and reporting

LC-08

In plain English
The long middle of the relationship: regular reports, review meetings and answering questions.
What happens
Reports go out on a fixed calendar. Review meetings, typically quarterly to annual, cover performance, positioning, risk, guideline compliance, service and outlook. Between meetings there are ad hoc questions, data requests from the consultant, regulatory reporting needs and operational changes. The relationship manager keeps the internal picture of the client current as people and priorities change.
Who leads
Relationship management.
Who supports
Client service and reporting teams, portfolio managers and product specialists for meetings, consultant relations.
What the junior person produces
  • Draft review pack reconciled to the official performance record
  • Meeting preparation note
  • Minutes and action log within two working days
  • Query log with response times
On the client side
Investment staff, trustees or committee, consultant, operations and finance. They need accurate information on time and plain explanations.
What good execution changes for the client
The client understands what it owns and why it has behaved as it has, and can govern the mandate with confidence.
Failure points
  • Late or wrong reports
  • Meetings that recite a pack and answer no questions
  • Actions that are not followed up
  • Losing touch when the client's staff change
Sales versus relationship management (illustrative; varies)
Stewardship. Sales stays informed because a well-served client is the main source of references and further mandates.
Timing
Years; this stage is most of the relationship.

Difficulties

LC-09

In plain English
Something goes wrong: performance disappoints, an error occurs, or key people leave.
What happens
Common triggers are sustained underperformance, a guideline breach or operational error, the departure of a portfolio manager, a change in the firm's ownership or strategy, or a change on the client's side such as a new consultant. The relationship manager establishes facts, informs the client early, brings the right senior people into the conversation and agrees remedies. Clients may place the manager under formal review or on a watch list.
Who leads
Relationship management, escalating to the team head and senior investment staff.
Who supports
Portfolio manager, risk, compliance and legal for breaches, operations for errors, consultant relations.
What the junior person produces
  • Chronology of facts for an incident
  • Draft holding statement and client note for compliance review
  • Attribution summary of what drove underperformance
  • Tracker of clients affected and who has been contacted
On the client side
Chief investment officer or pensions manager, trustee chair, consultant. They need the truth quickly, a clear account of cause and remedy, and evidence that it will not recur.
What good execution changes for the client
The client hears bad news first from the manager, understands it, and can make a reasoned decision to stay, reduce or leave.
Failure points
  • The client learning of a problem from the press or its consultant
  • Defensive or evasive explanations
  • Predicting a recovery that cannot be promised
  • Compensation or remediation handled slowly
Sales versus relationship management (illustrative; varies)
Stewardship under stress. A badly handled difficulty also damages origination, because consultants remember.
Timing
Unpredictable; a formal review can last several quarters.

Additional allocations and cross-sell

LC-10

In plain English
The client considers giving the manager more money or a second, different mandate.
What happens
A need emerges from the client's changing strategy, for instance moving towards lower-risk assets, adding private markets or consolidating managers. The relationship manager recognises it, tests whether the firm has a suitable capability, and introduces the right colleagues. Even for an existing client a larger or new mandate may need a formal process. Sometimes the right conclusion is that the client should not add.
Who leads
Relationship management or sales, according to the firm's coverage model.
Who supports
Product specialists for the new capability, the original salesperson, pricing for relationship-level fee terms.
What the junior person produces
  • Opportunity note: the client's stated need, evidence and timing
  • Updated client map and exposure summary across all mandates
  • Fee illustration including any breakpoint effect of larger assets
  • Briefing for the specialist who has never met the client
On the client side
Investment staff and consultant. They need a proposal that reflects what the manager already knows about them and respects any limit on exposure to one firm.
What good execution changes for the client
The client gets a relevant idea at the right time from people who understand its situation, and is not pestered with irrelevant ones.
Failure points
  • Pitching while an existing problem is unresolved
  • Proposing a product because it is a firm priority, not because it fits
  • Internal dispute over credit delaying the response
  • Ignoring the client's manager-concentration limits
Sales versus relationship management (illustrative; varies)
The clearest overlap between origination and stewardship. Firms differ on who leads and who is credited.
Timing
Opportunistic; depends on the client's strategy cycle.

Formal review or re-tender

LC-11

In plain English
The client deliberately tests whether the manager should keep the mandate.
What happens
Many asset owners review managers on a fixed cycle or after a trigger. The review may be a desk-based assessment by the consultant, a re-presentation to trustees, or a full re-tender against competitors. Public-sector bodies may be required to re-procure. The incumbent must show its record, how it handled problems, and why it remains the right choice for the client's current needs, which may have changed since appointment.
Who leads
Relationship management, with sales where the review is a competitive tender.
Who supports
Portfolio manager, RFP team, consultant relations, team head.
What the junior person produces
  • Incumbent record: performance, service statistics, incidents and how they were resolved
  • Summary of how the client's needs have changed since appointment
  • Re-tender response using the client's own history, not library text
  • Fee comparison and options for approval
On the client side
Trustees or committee, consultant, sometimes procurement. They need a fair basis for comparison and may want to see the manager challenged.
What good execution changes for the client
The client reaffirms or changes its decision on current evidence, with the incumbent having given an honest account of its record.
Failure points
  • Complacency: treating the review as a formality
  • Defending the original mandate when the client's needs have moved on
  • Fee concessions offered only under threat, which damages trust
  • A new consultant with no history with the firm
Sales versus relationship management (illustrative; varies)
Both. The relationship manager holds the evidence; sales brings competitive discipline.
Timing
Months; the cycle between reviews is typically several years.

Renewal or exit

LC-12

In plain English
The mandate continues on refreshed terms, shrinks, or ends.
What happens
Renewal may bring revised guidelines, fees or reporting. Exit can be full or partial and has many causes: performance, a change in the client's strategy such as a pension scheme buying insurance for its liabilities, consolidation, a merger, or a new decision-maker's preferences. On exit the manager cooperates with the transition: providing data, selling or transferring assets in an orderly way, final reporting and fee reconciliation. How a firm behaves on the way out affects whether it is invited back.
Who leads
Relationship management.
Who supports
Operations, portfolio manager, legal, the incoming transition manager where one is used.
What the junior person produces
  • Transition-out checklist and final reporting schedule
  • Final fee reconciliation support
  • Lessons-learned note recorded in the CRM
  • Updated contact record so the relationship can resume later
On the client side
Investment staff, operations, custodian, incoming manager or insurer. They need a clean, cooperative handover.
What good execution changes for the client
The client leaves or renews with its assets and records in order and without avoidable cost.
Failure points
  • Obstructive or slow cooperation after notice
  • No record of why the client left
  • Treating a rational client decision as a failure to be argued with
  • Losing contact with people who will be decision-makers elsewhere
Sales versus relationship management (illustrative; varies)
Stewardship to the end, then back to origination: a former client is a future prospect.
Timing
Notice periods are set by the contract; transitions take weeks to months.

Wealth-intermediary path

Gatekeeper research

TPW-01

In plain English
A wealth manager's fund research team studies the fund before anyone is allowed to buy it.
What happens
The fund selector or research analyst screens a peer group, requests data and a questionnaire, meets the portfolio manager and scores the fund against competitors. The asset manager's salesperson supplies information in the selector's format and arranges access to the investment team.
Who leads
Third-party wealth sales.
Who supports
Investment specialist, portfolio manager, marketing and data teams.
What the junior person produces
  • Selector briefing
  • Data in the selector's template, checked to the factsheet
  • Peer-group comparison
  • Meeting notes with open questions
On the client side
Fund selector or research analyst (the gatekeeper), who answers to an investment committee.
What good execution changes for the client
The selector can assess the fund efficiently and accurately against alternatives.
Failure points
  • Data in the wrong format or late
  • A portfolio manager who does not answer the question asked
  • Pitching a fund the firm wants to sell instead of the one the selector is researching
Sales versus relationship management (illustrative; varies)
Origination.
Timing
Weeks to many months; reviews follow the selector's calendar.

Buy-list or approved-list decision

TPW-02

In plain English
The intermediary's investment committee decides whether the fund may be used.
What happens
The selector presents a recommendation to an investment committee. If approved, the fund joins a buy list, recommended list or model portfolio universe. Approval is permission to buy; it is not a purchase.
Who leads
The intermediary's committee decides; sales responds to final queries.
Who supports
Legal and product teams for share-class and fee terms.
What the junior person produces
  • Answers to committee follow-up questions
  • Share-class and fee summary
  • Record of the decision and its conditions in the CRM
On the client side
Investment committee, head of research, sometimes compliance.
What good execution changes for the client
The committee decides on complete information and understands where the fund fits and where it does not.
Failure points
  • Assuming approval equals assets
  • Unclear role for the fund in portfolios
  • Share class or fee terms not agreed in time
Sales versus relationship management (illustrative; varies)
Origination, shading into stewardship immediately.
Timing
A committee cycle.

Platform availability and set-up

TPW-03

In plain English
The fund must be technically available where advisers actually place trades.
What happens
The right share class is listed on the investment platforms the intermediary uses, with correct identifiers, charges and documents. Distribution agreements are completed. Data feeds to the platform and to research tools are tested.
Who leads
Product and distribution operations, coordinated by the relationship manager or sales.
Who supports
Legal, fund administrator, data vendors.
What the junior person produces
  • Platform availability checklist by share class
  • Document pack: key information, factsheet, prospectus links
  • Data-feed check against official figures
On the client side
Platform operations, the intermediary's operations and compliance staff.
What good execution changes for the client
An adviser who wants to buy the fund can do so without friction, at the correct price.
Failure points
  • Approved fund not available on the platform advisers use
  • Wrong charges displayed
  • Missing documents blocking trades
Sales versus relationship management (illustrative; varies)
Operational seam between the two.
Timing
Days to weeks, depending on the platform.

Adviser and portfolio-manager adoption

TPW-04

In plain English
The people who run client portfolios decide, one by one, whether to use the approved fund.
What happens
Advisers, discretionary portfolio managers or the team running model portfolios choose among approved funds. The asset manager supports adoption with briefings, plain-language material and access to specialists. In centrally run model portfolios one decision can move large sums; in adviser-led firms adoption is gradual.
Who leads
Third-party wealth sales, with relationship management for existing holders.
Who supports
Investment specialists, marketing, events.
What the junior person produces
  • Adviser briefing material
  • Event logistics and attendee follow-up
  • Adoption tracker by office or desk
  • Log of objections heard
On the client side
Advisers, discretionary managers, model-portfolio team; behind them, the end investor whose interests the intermediary must serve.
What good execution changes for the client
Advisers understand what the fund is for and can explain it accurately to their own clients.
Failure points
  • Material too technical for adviser conversations
  • No clear reason to choose the fund over an existing holding
  • Coverage spread too thinly across many offices
Sales versus relationship management (illustrative; varies)
Blended.
Timing
Months to years; often never complete.

Flows

TPW-05

In plain English
Money arrives, and leaves, in many small transactions.
What happens
Subscriptions and redemptions pass through platforms daily. The manager sees aggregate flows by intermediary, with limited sight of individual end investors. Flows respond to performance, market sentiment, model-portfolio rebalancing and the intermediary's own client growth.
Who leads
No single lead; sales and relationship management both monitor.
Who supports
Data and business-intelligence teams.
What the junior person produces
  • Weekly flow report by intermediary and fund
  • Explanation of unusual movements
  • List of approved-but-unused funds
On the client side
End investors through advisers and platforms.
What good execution changes for the client
The manager notices early when a holder is reducing and can ask why.
Failure points
  • Reading gross sales without redemptions
  • Mistaking a model rebalance for a change of view
  • No follow-up on unexplained outflows
Sales versus relationship management (illustrative; varies)
Blended.
Timing
Continuous.

Monitoring and ongoing due diligence

TPW-06

In plain English
The gatekeeper keeps checking that the fund still deserves its place.
What happens
Selectors review held funds on a schedule and after triggers such as underperformance, a manager change or a fund growing too large. The asset manager provides updates, access to the team and prompt notice of changes. For funds reaching retail investors in the UK, the manufacturer and the distributor each carry Consumer Duty obligations, including on fair value, so value assessments and target-market information are part of the exchange.
Who leads
Third-party wealth relationship management.
Who supports
Portfolio managers, product governance, compliance.
What the junior person produces
  • Annual due-diligence update pack
  • Change notifications to all holders
  • Watch-list tracker with decision dates
  • Responses to value and target-market queries
On the client side
Fund research team, investment committee, compliance.
What good execution changes for the client
The intermediary can keep using the fund with confidence, or act promptly if it should not.
Failure points
  • Holders learning of a manager change from the press
  • Slow or incomplete responses to review questions
  • Treating the annual review as routine
Sales versus relationship management (illustrative; varies)
Stewardship.
Timing
Annual cycle plus triggers.

Removal or replacement

TPW-07

In plain English
The fund is taken off the list, or the intermediary itself changes.
What happens
A fund may be downgraded, put on hold or removed after poor performance, a team change, a cheaper alternative, list consolidation, or the intermediary being acquired and its lists merged. Removal can trigger rapid redemptions from model portfolios. The manager supports an orderly exit and records the reason.
Who leads
Relationship management.
Who supports
Sales (for alternative funds that may fit), operations, liquidity management within the fund.
What the junior person produces
  • Record of the stated reason and the real one if different
  • Redemption forecast for the portfolio manager
  • Note on whether another capability might genuinely fit
On the client side
Investment committee, selectors, advisers who must explain the change to their clients.
What good execution changes for the client
End investors are moved without avoidable cost and the intermediary remains willing to consider the manager again.
Failure points
  • Arguing with the decision instead of understanding it
  • Immediately pitching a replacement fund
  • No lessons recorded
Sales versus relationship management (illustrative; varies)
Stewardship, then origination begins again.
Timing
Can be sudden.

Appendix G · Roles and decision rights

General industry practice, not a Goldman Sachs job architecture.

Summer Analyst (intern)

≈ Supported inference ROLE-SUMMER-ANALYST

Purpose

Appendix H · Why-trees and personal ledger

In the application each level opens only when you click it, so you can answer before reading. Here every level is printed.

Why asset management?

Layer C · personal fit WT-am

Opening claim: I want to work in asset management.

What this tree does not prove

This tree shows what is structurally distinctive about asset management and which of those features might appeal to me. It does not prove that I would enjoy client coverage inside it, and nothing in it has been tested by doing the job.

Why 1 What are you pointing at in asset management that is not simply 'finance'?
Claim
I think I am pointing at the fact that the product is a continuing responsibility for someone else's money, not a single transaction.
Plain-English meaning
A manager is hired to look after money for years and is paid a percentage of it for as long as it keeps the job.
The actual task
Checking a quarterly review pack before it goes to a client, and helping answer the client's question about why the portfolio behaved as it did. The same client receives the next pack three months later.
Reasoning or source
General industry mechanics: management fees accrue on assets over time, so the commercial model rewards keeping a mandate as well as winning it (see the chapter on mandates and economics).
Strongest objection
Banking and markets also have repeat clients, so recurring business is not unique. And the 'continuing responsibility' for the money sits with portfolio managers, not with a junior in client coverage.
Where the claim stops being valid
True for segregated mandates and long-held fund positions. Much weaker where a wealth platform can redeem a fund holding within days.
Why 2 Repeat clients exist in banking and markets too. What does the long holding period change about the work you would actually do?
Claim
I think it changes what a mistake costs and what gets noticed. The work is judged across review cycles, so accuracy and follow-through are visible later, not only the pitch.
Plain-English meaning
If I get a figure wrong in a report, or forget something that was promised in a meeting, the same client sees it next quarter.
The actual task
Reconciling performance and attribution figures in a pack against their source; keeping a list of actions from a client meeting and closing each one by the date given.
Reasoning or source
Repeated interaction gives each side a record of the other's behaviour (see the chapter on client relationships). This is reasoning, not a disclosed fact about any firm.
Strongest objection
That is a preference for accountable detail. Fund operations, audit and fund accounting offer that more purely. It is not yet an argument for asset management.
Where the claim stops being valid
Does not hold where coverage staff rotate quickly or where the client rarely reads what it is sent.
Why 3 A preference for accountable detail fits operations or audit. Why do you need the investment content at all?
Claim
Answer A: I want the detail to be about markets and portfolios. I would rather explain why a credit portfolio lagged its benchmark than reconcile a ledger.
Plain-English meaning
The subject matter, how money is invested and why results differ, is itself what I want to spend my days on.
The actual task
Reading a portfolio manager's commentary and an attribution report, then writing two paragraphs a trustee without a finance background can follow.
Reasoning or source
Untested unless my evidence ledger shows that I chose investment content when nothing required me to. Studying economics is weak evidence: many people study it and prefer other work.
Strongest objection
If the content is the draw, research or portfolio management offer more of it at first hand. Coverage offers a translated, second-hand version.
Where the claim stops being valid
Valid only if I am content to explain decisions that I did not make.
Why 4 If the investment content is the draw, why not research or portfolio management, where you would do the analysis yourself?
Claim
I think I prefer breadth across many strategies, and the work of matching them to a client's problem, over depth in one security or one asset class. I have not tested whether breadth would start to feel shallow after a year.
Plain-English meaning
Coverage people need to know a fair amount about many strategies. Portfolio managers know a great deal about one.
The actual task
Preparing for a review with a pension scheme that holds three different strategies, and knowing enough about each to decide which specialist has to be in the room.
Reasoning or source
A structural feature of coverage roles as publicly described (see the chapter on the role): generalist coverage with specialists brought in. That it would suit me is my inference.
Strongest objection
'Breadth' can be a polite word for never being the expert in the room. Decision rights over the portfolio sit with someone else.
Where the claim stops being valid
Fails if I find that I need to have made the call myself in order to feel ownership of the result.
Why 5 You would be explaining and defending decisions other people made. Why would that satisfy you instead of frustrating you?
Claim
My honest position is that I do not know yet. The assumption I am making is that my sense of ownership would come from the client's understanding and decision, for example a trustee who can now explain their own portfolio, and not from the investment call.
Plain-English meaning
What I would 'own' is whether the client understood and decided well. I would not own whether the fund beat its benchmark.
The actual task
Writing the follow-up note after a difficult performance meeting. The client's next questions show whether the explanation was understood.
Reasoning or source
This is an assumption about my own motivation. Layer C, untested.
Strongest objection
When performance is poor for reasons outside my control, 'the client understood why' may feel like thin compensation, and the client may leave anyway.
Where the claim stops being valid
Holds only if I can separate the quality of my own work from an outcome I did not control.
Why 6 What would you observe in yourself that would show this assumption is wrong?
Claim
If, on occasions when I have explained someone else's work, I mostly wanted to go and redo the analysis myself, that points towards research. If I mostly cared whether the other person could now act on it, that supports coverage. I need to check which is true instead of asserting it.
Plain-English meaning
There is a factual answer in my own history, and I should go and look for it.
The actual task
No job task: this is a check against the personal evidence ledger.
Reasoning or source
Reflection question, see the ledger section of this chapter.
Strongest objection
Memory flatters. I may recall whichever version suits the application I am writing.
Where the claim stops being valid
One or two episodes are weak evidence either way. A summer internship is the first real test.
Why 3 A preference for accountable detail fits operations or audit. Why do you need the investment content at all?
Claim
Answer B: honestly the investment content is secondary for me. What I like is being the reliable point of contact in a commercially serious setting.
Plain-English meaning
I may like the service and responsibility, with markets as the setting and not the point.
The actual task
Owning a client query inbox: logging the question, routing it to the team that can answer it, chasing the answer, and replying accurately by the time promised.
Reasoning or source
This is a legitimate preference. But it changes which arguments I am entitled to use.
Strongest objection
Then account management in software or professional services gives the same satisfaction with less technical study and without my employer's revenue moving with the markets.
Where the claim stops being valid
If this is my answer, I should stop claiming fascination with markets in an interview. It will not survive two follow-up questions.
Why 4 Then why asset management, and not account management in any business-to-business industry?
Claim
The only non-circular answers I can find are these. First, the stakes: the clients are institutions with obligations to pensioners, policyholders or beneficiaries. Second, the learning curve is steeper and longer. If neither matters to me in practice, I should describe asset management as a good setting for the work I like, not as a calling.
Plain-English meaning
I would be choosing the setting for what rides on the work and how much there is to learn, and not for love of investing.
The actual task
Learning enough about liability-driven investment to route a pension client's collateral question to the right desk and to tell whether the answer that comes back is complete.
Reasoning or source
An honest, narrower claim is more defensible than a broad one I cannot support.
Strongest objection
'High stakes' and 'steep learning' also describe law, medicine and engineering. I still have not explained why finance.
Where the claim stops being valid
This branch ends in an acknowledged limit: the appeal is the role type. The industry is a secondary preference, and I should say so.

Counterfactual tests

Would this appeal remain without the Goldman Sachs name?
If yes
The appeal is about the industry's structure: continuing responsibility, review cycles, the investment content. Those exist at any manager.
If no
Then I am drawn to an employer, and should work through the 'Why Goldman Sachs?' tree before claiming an interest in asset management.
What that suggests
Whether my reason is about the industry or about one firm.
Would this appeal remain without unusually high pay?
If yes
I would accept ordinary graduate pay for this work. That supports the content or the responsibility as the real draw.
If no
Pay is doing most of the work. Pay is a legitimate reason, but it does not distinguish asset management from other well-paid careers and cannot be the answer to 'why this'.
What that suggests
Whether I would choose the daily tasks at a typical professional salary.
Would this appeal remain if the first year involved extensive preparation and administration?
If yes
I accept that the first year is mostly checking, formatting and chasing, and I see it as how the material is learned.
If no
I am attracted to the senior version of the job. I need evidence that I do careful preparatory work well when nobody is watching.
What that suggests
Whether I like the apprenticeship, or only the destination.
Would this appeal remain if the client declined after months of work?
If yes
I can treat lost business as part of a long cycle. The industry's slow pace suits me.
If no
I may need faster and more frequent feedback than institutional asset management gives. Markets roles or shorter-cycle distribution may suit better.
What that suggests
My tolerance for long, uncertain cycles.
Would this appeal remain if the client's best decision meant withdrawing money?
If yes
I see the manager's job as serving the client's objective, even when that shrinks the assets managed.
If no
I am thinking of clients as assets to be held. That will show in how I answer questions on suitability and on when a client should leave.
What that suggests
Whether I have accepted the central conflict of the business or am avoiding it.
Valuable is not the same as enjoyable
That pension schemes and insurers need their assets managed well is a fact about the world. It says nothing about whether I would enjoy checking attribution tables and writing follow-up notes, which is what the first years consist of.
An answer that points to a different role
If the investment content is what I want and I need to make the calls myself, research or portfolio management fits better. If the content is incidental, account management in another industry would serve the same preference, and I should ask why I am putting myself through finance recruitment.
Where the tree ends
Acknowledged uncertainty resting on an explicit assumption: I assume I would take ownership from the client's understanding and not from the investment decision. I have not tested this.

Why institutional clients?

Layer C · personal fit WT-inst

Opening claim: I am drawn to institutional clients more than to individuals.

What this tree does not prove

This tree examines what is different about serving institutions. It does not show that institutions are better clients, or that I have the patience their decision cycles require.

Why 1 What is different about an institution as a client that you actually want?
Claim
I think it is that the client has a defined obligation, such as pensions to pay, a spending rule to meet or claims to cover. 'What do they need?' then has an answer that can be analysed and not merely guessed.
Plain-English meaning
A pension scheme owes specific payments on specific dates. You can read about them and reason about what the money must do.
The actual task
Before a meeting, reading a scheme's annual report and its statement of investment principles to find its funding position, cash-flow needs and stated investment beliefs.
Reasoning or source
General feature of institutional investors (see the foundations chapter). That I find it attractive is my inference about myself.
Strongest objection
Individuals also have defined goals: retirement, a house, school fees. And an institution's written objectives often conceal committee politics and individual career risk.
Where the claim stops being valid
Breaks down for clients whose objectives are vague or not public, such as some family offices and some sovereign investors.
Why 2 Institutional decisions are made by committees, with politics and career risk. Does that make the 'analysable need' a fiction?
Claim
Partly. I think the real client is a governance process: trustees, an in-house investment officer and an external consultant, each with different constraints. What interests me is working out what each of them needs before the answer can be yes. I should admit that this is closer to stakeholder mapping than to finance.
Plain-English meaning
The 'client' is several people who must all agree, and each worries about something different.
The actual task
Drafting a one-page map before a pitch: who sits on the investment committee, who advises them, how the consultant rates the strategy, and who lost money in this asset class before.
Reasoning or source
How institutional selection works in general (see the chapter on teams and clients). The interest I claim in it is untested.
Strongest objection
Then the job is navigating bureaucracy. A decision can take over a year and be stopped by a consultant's research team that I never meet.
Where the claim stops being valid
If mapping stakeholders sounds tedious to me and not interesting, this tree stops here and the opening claim is probably about status.
Why 3 A decision can take more than a year and fail for reasons outside your control. Why choose slow cycles over fast feedback?
Claim
Answer A: I think I prefer few, large, slow decisions where preparation compounds, because the tenth piece of knowledge about a client makes the first nine more useful.
Plain-English meaning
I would rather go deep on a small number of big decisions than handle many small quick ones.
The actual task
Maintaining an account plan for one prospect across a year: each meeting note, each consultant comment and each change in their funding position added to the same file.
Reasoning or source
A stated preference. It needs evidence from how I have actually behaved on long projects.
Strongest objection
Slow cycles mean months with nothing to show. People who say they like long games often mean that they like having won one.
Where the claim stops being valid
Only valid if I have stayed motivated through long stretches without external feedback.
Why 4 What evidence do you have that you stay motivated for months without a visible win?
Claim
I am not sure that I have any. The evidence would be a long piece of work where I kept the quality up without outside feedback. I need to check my ledger for one. If there is none, this is a hope and not a preference.
Plain-English meaning
I may be describing the person I would like to be.
The actual task
No job task: a check against the personal evidence ledger.
Reasoning or source
Reflection question, see the ledger section of this chapter.
Strongest objection
Even with such evidence, a university project is not a twelve-month sales cycle with a manager asking for pipeline updates.
Where the claim stops being valid
Evidence from study or a placement transfers imperfectly to a commercial setting.
Why 5 Private wealth advisers also keep clients for decades, with one decision-maker and quicker answers. Why not that?
Claim
I think I would prefer the counterparty to be a professional buyer who can test me technically, over depending on personal rapport with one principal. That is a guess about private wealth that I have not tested, and it may underrate how technical private clients and their advisers are.
Plain-English meaning
I would like the person across the table to be paid to scrutinise me.
The actual task
Answering a due diligence questionnaire or a consultant's research questions, where vague answers are noticed and marked down.
Reasoning or source
My inference about two client types. I have no direct evidence about private wealth.
Strongest objection
Professional buyers also mean procurement processes, fee compression and less personal recognition. Some people find private clients more rewarding for exactly that reason.
Where the claim stops being valid
This is a preference between two legitimate models. It is not a ranking.
Why 6 And if the answer after a year of work is no?
Claim
Then what remains is what I learned about that client and the standing I built with their consultant. That is only worth something if the firm values pipeline quality as well as closed business. I do not know how performance in these teams is measured.
Plain-English meaning
A 'no' still leaves knowledge and reputation, but only if someone counts them.
The actual task
Writing the loss review: why we were not selected, what the consultant said, when the mandate next comes up for review.
Reasoning or source
How these teams measure performance is not publicly established.
Strongest objection
'I learned something' is what people say about failures. Several in a row would test whether I believe it.
Where the claim stops being valid
Acknowledged uncertainty: I do not know my tolerance for repeated, unexplained rejection.
Why 3 A decision can take more than a year and fail for reasons outside your control. Why choose slow cycles over fast feedback?
Claim
Answer B: honestly, I like faster feedback. I may be choosing 'institutional' because it sounds more serious.
Plain-English meaning
The pull may be status and not the working rhythm.
The actual task
None. This is about my reason, not a task.
Reasoning or source
Being honest here is useful. It redirects me without disqualifying me.
Strongest objection
If I say this to myself, I should not then say the opposite in an interview.
Where the claim stops being valid
Stands unless I can find a reason grounded in the work.
Why 4 Is 'more serious' a reason about the work, or about status?
Claim
Mostly status. The version grounded in the work is narrower: larger tickets bring more specialist involvement and more technical conversation per client. If what I want is pace, third-party wealth distribution, with many fund selectors, shorter cycles and more frequent contact, or markets sales could fit better, and they are not lesser choices.
Plain-English meaning
If I like quick feedback, there are client-facing roles designed around it.
The actual task
In a wealth distribution seat: preparing for several fund-selector meetings in one week, each on a different fund and each with quick feedback on whether the fund stays on the buy list.
Reasoning or source
General industry pattern (see the chapter comparing team business models). Supported inference, not a Goldman Sachs fact.
Strongest objection
Wealth distribution has its own slow parts. Getting onto an approved list can take as long as an institutional search.
Where the claim stops being valid
This branch ends in a redirected preference: client-facing, yes; institutional specifically, unproven.

Counterfactual tests

Would this appeal remain without the Goldman Sachs name?
If yes
My interest is in how institutions decide. That exists at every manager and at investment consultants.
If no
'Institutional' may be standing in for 'prestigious firm'. I should ask whether I would take a retail-facing job at the same firm.
What that suggests
Whether the client type or the employer is the attraction.
Would this appeal remain without unusually high pay?
If yes
I find the client's problem interesting at ordinary pay.
If no
The institutional label may be a proxy for expected earnings. Any pay difference between segments is not publicly established.
What that suggests
Whether I would still pick this client type if all segments paid the same.
Would this appeal remain if the first year involved extensive preparation and administration?
If yes
I would read scheme accounts and build stakeholder maps as the main content of my first year.
If no
I like the idea of the boardroom and not the preparation that earns a place in it.
What that suggests
Whether desk research on clients is itself attractive to me.
Would this appeal remain if the client declined after months of work?
If yes
I expect most searches to be lost and can still value the process.
If no
The long, uncertain institutional cycle is a poor fit. Shorter-cycle distribution may suit me better.
What that suggests
Whether I chose slow cycles knowingly.
Would this appeal remain if the client's best decision meant withdrawing money?
If yes
I understand that a scheme moving towards buy-out should hold less with an asset manager, and that helping it do so is still the job.
If no
I see institutional clients as large pools to be captured. That contradicts my own opening claim about analysing their needs.
What that suggests
